'''''Acacia verticillata''''' ('''prickly Moses'''; '''prickly-leaved wattle'''; '''star-leaved acacia'''; '''prickly mimosa'''; '''whorl-leaved acacia''') is a [[perennial]] shrub to small [[tree]] native to south eastern [[Australia]].

==Description==
The shrub or tree can grow to a maximum height of around {{cvt|10|m}} and has a spreading habit. The branchlets have bristly prickling [[stipule]]s with a length of {{cvt|0.5|to|2|mm}} in length. Like most species of ''Acacia'' it has [[phyllode]]s rather than true leaves. The evergreen phyllodes grow in bundles that are all crowded together and are whorled that have a linear or lanceolate shape with a length of {{cvt|5|to|25|mm}} and a width of {{cvt|1|to|7|mm}}. The phyllodes are [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]], pungent and rigid with one main visible vein.<ref name=www>{{cite web|url=http://worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/verticillata.php|title=''Acacia verticillata''|access-date=21 March 2020|work=WorldWideWattle|publisher=[[Western Australian Herbarium]]}}</ref> It blooms between July and December producing simple [[inflorescence]]s on glabrous stalks with a length of {{cvt|2|to|5|mm}}. The ovoid the spherical flower-spikes have a length of up to {{cvt|4.5|cm}} with densely pack light yellow coloured flowers. The compressed a linear [[seed pod]]s that form after flowering are barely constricted between each of the seeds. The pods are {{cvt|2|to|8|cm}} in length and have a width of {{cvt|3|to|5|mm}} and have quite thin valves. The elliptic shaped seeds are around {{cvt|3|to|4|mm}} in length and have a filamentous funicle that folds and thickens into a turbinate [[aril]].<ref name=www/>

==Taxonomy==
The species was first described by [[Charles Louis L'Héritier de Brutelle]] in 1806 as part of [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]]s work ''[[Species Plantarum]]''. It was reclassified as ''Racosperma verticillatum'' by [[Leslie Pedley]] in 2003 then transferred back to genus ''Acacia'' in 2006.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bie.ala.org.au/species/https://id.biodiversity.org.au/taxon/apni/51287115#names|title=''Acacia verticillata'' (L'Hér.) Willd.|access-date=21 March 2020|work=Atlas of Living Australia|publisher=[[Global Biodiversity Information Facility]]}}</ref>

Four [[subspecies]] are known:
* ''Acacia verticillata'' subsp. ''verticillata''
* ''Acacia verticillata'' subsp. ''ruscifolia''
* ''Acacia verticillata'' subsp. ''cephalantha''
* ''Acacia verticillata'' subsp. ''ovoidea''<ref name=www/>

==Distribution==
''A. verticillata'' is [[endemism|endemic]] to [[New South Wales]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[South Australia]] and [[Tasmania]].<ref name="ILDIS"/> The species is a common understorey shrub in both wet and dry [[sclerophyll]] forests as well as scrub and heath. In coastal environments it will often have much wider leaves as opposed to the regular needle-like nature of inland specimens. The range of the plant extends from the [[Gulf St Vincent]] in South Australia throughout the  south-eastern parts and into southern and south eastern Victoria and far south-eastern New South Wales and Tasmania including the islands in [[Bass Strait]] where it is situated in saline, riparian and submontane areas.<ref name=www/>

==Uses==
Prickly Moses is sold commercially for cultivation and can grow in full sun or part shade in a variety of locations including plains, hills and footslopes as a second line from the coast. It will grow in clay or loam soils that are [[alkaline]], neutral or [[acid]]ic and will tolerate [[drought]], water logging and a moderate frost. It is regarded as an excellent habitat for birds but is highly flammable and not recommended for near houses in bushfire prone areas.<ref name=ps>{{cite web|url=http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/3692|title=''Acacia verticillata'' Prickly Moses|access-date=21 March 2020|work=Plant Selector|publisher=[[Botanic Gardens of South Australia]]}}</ref>
[[Indigenous Australian]]s used the fibre from the plant to make fishing lines.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Middle_Storey/Shrubs_1_12m_-10m/Acacia_verticillata_ssp_verticillata|title=''Acacia verticillata'' ssp. ''verticillata''|access-date=21 March 2020|publisher=[[Yarra Ranges Shire Council]]|year=2009|archive-date=21 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200321092036/http://fe.yarraranges.vic.gov.au/Residents/Trees_Vegetation/Yarra_Ranges_Plant_Directory/Yarra_Ranges_Local_Plant_Directory/Middle_Storey/Shrubs_1_12m_-10m/Acacia_verticillata_ssp_verticillata}}</ref>

==In popular culture==
On 1 September 2016, the [[Reserve Bank of Australia]] released a replacement of the polymer five dollar note which includes a depiction of ''Acacia verticillata'' (subspecies ''ovoidea)''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://banknotes.rba.gov.au/australias-banknotes/banknotes-in-circulation/five-dollar/|title=RBA Banknotes: $5 Banknote|website=banknotes.rba.gov.au|access-date=2016-09-03}}</ref>
